planting.note: Set container-grown plants out in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this very cold-hardy elepidote was named the ARS 2024 Rhododendron of the Year for the Mid-Atlantic region.

directions: Site this compact elepidote in dappled or filtered light with consistently moist, acidic soil and a thick mulch layer to protect its shallow roots. Rounded trusses open pale pink and fade to white, each petal marked with distinctive burgundy flecks near the throat, in mid-spring. It was chosen by the American Rhododendron Society as its 2024 Rhododendron of the Year for the Mid-Atlantic region for its reliable bloom and exceptional cold tolerance. Water during dry spells and avoid disturbing the root zone once established.

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in a woodland setting with filtered light; this yakushimanum selection was the ARS 2020 Rhododendron of the Year (Elepidote) for the North East USA and Canada region.

directions: A selection of the species Rhododendron yakushimanum, this rounded, multi-stemmed shrub carries the species' trademark felted, silvery new growth and dense habit. Buds open pale purplish pink and age to white, lightly touched with yellow-green dorsal spotting, giving trusses a soft, misty look that inspired the cultivar's name. The American Rhododendron Society recognized it as its 2020 Rhododendron of the Year for the Northeast and Canada. Give it humus-rich, well-drained soil and steady moisture, since like most yakushimanum forms it resents both drought and waterlogging.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this tetraploid Pennington hybrid was named the ARS 2021 Rhododendron of the Year (Elepidote) for the Southeast USA region.

directions: Bred as a tetraploid, this hybrid carries unusually thick, fir-green leaves and sturdy stems that help it stand up to Southeastern summer heat better than many elepidotes. Vivid purplish-red flowers with a darker blotch open in funnel-shaped trusses in mid-spring and hold their color well. It earned ARS Rhododendron of the Year honors for the Southeast region in 2021. Grow it in well-drained, acidic soil with a cooling mulch layer and avoid exposing it to harsh winter wind.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this sun-tolerant lepidote was named the ARS 2021 Rhododendron of the Year (Lepidote) for the Southeast USA region.

directions: This large lepidote carries bold trusses of dark pink flowers marked with red-spotted throats, and its small, leathery leaves turn an attractive bronze-mahogany through winter rather than dropping. It tolerates more direct sun than most rhododendrons, making it a dependable choice for brighter garden edges in the Southeast, where it was named the ARS Rhododendron of the Year in 2021. Keep soil consistently moist and acidic, and mulch to buffer root temperature swings.

planting.note: Plant in spring in moist, acidic, humus-rich soil in partial shade; this Dexter hybrid was named the ARS 2015 Rhododendron of the Year (Elepidote) for the South Central USA region.

directions: Bred by the Cape Cod amateur hybridizer Charles O. Dexter, this upright, rounded shrub opens wide funnel-shaped flowers in deep purplish pink that fade through lighter pink to nearly white as they age, giving each truss a two-toned effect. It was selected as the ARS Rhododendron of the Year for the South Central region in 2015. Provide acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter and keep it out of harsh afternoon sun in warmer parts of its range.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this Nearing hybrid lepidote was named the ARS 2015 Rhododendron of the Year (Lepidote) for the South Central USA region.

directions: One of the best-known Nearing hybrids, this compact, rounded shrub bears small, aromatic olive-green leaves that turn bronze in fall and apricot-tinged white flowers that soften to pale pink as they age. Exceptional cold tolerance and a tidy habit earned it recognition as the ARS Rhododendron of the Year for the South Central region in 2015. It thrives in acidic, humus-rich soil with reliable moisture and benefits from light shade during the hottest part of the day.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil in partial shade; this elepidote was named the ARS 2008 Rhododendron of the Year for the Northwest USA region.

directions: This rounded, early-midseason bloomer produces light greenish-yellow flowers set off by a dark red blotch, a color combination that stands out against the glossy evergreen foliage. The American Rhododendron Society named it its 2008 Rhododendron of the Year for the Northwest. Give it consistently moist, acidic soil and dappled shade, and mulch well to keep the root zone cool through summer.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this lepidote was named the ARS 2008 Rhododendron of the Year for the Northwest USA region and suits milder-winter gardens.

directions: Early-spring flowers in a saturated violet-blue, with wavy to frilly lobes and contrasting brownish-orange anthers, make this compact lepidote a striking accent in a mild-climate border. It was named the ARS Rhododendron of the Year for the Northwest region in 2008. Plant it where afternoon shade is available, use acidic, humus-rich soil, and keep moisture steady since it is less cold-tolerant than many hardy hybrids.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this exceptionally cold-hardy lepidote was named the ARS 2020 Rhododendron of the Year (Lepidote) for the North East USA and Canada region.

directions: Lightly fragrant, double, purplish-red flowers in a widely funnel shape cover this hardy lepidote in early spring, giving an unusually full look for a small-leaf rhododendron. Its outstanding cold tolerance earned it ARS Rhododendron of the Year honors for the Northeast and Canada region in 2020. It performs best in acidic, well-drained soil with partial shade and needs little pruning to keep its naturally neat shape.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this RHS Award of Garden Merit lepidote is a long-standing ARS chapter Proven Performer prized for reliability and fragrance.

directions: A carolinianum-group selection, this low, wide-spreading shrub grows roughly twice as broad as it is tall and produces broadly funnel-shaped, sometimes fragrant white flowers lightly spotted with greenish yellow on the dorsal lobe. Its toughness and dependable bloom have made it a repeat entry on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists across multiple regions. Leaves can take on a bronze cast in brighter sun, so dappled light keeps the foliage its richest dark green. Grow it in humus-rich, acidic soil with steady moisture.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, gritty, well-drained soil; this dwarf lepidote bred by Greer Gardens is a frequently cited ARS chapter Proven Performer for rock gardens.

directions: This diminutive rock-garden rhododendron bears bright pink buds that open to blush pink and fade almost to white, often showing two or three shades on the plant at once. Its tight, mounding habit and small burgundy-tinged leaves make it a frequent pick on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists for compact gardens. Give it sharply drained, acidic soil since dwarf lepidotes are more prone to root rot than larger hybrids, and site it where winter sun won't scorch the foliage.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, gritty, well-drained soil; this dwarf yellow-flowered lepidote is a widely listed ARS chapter Proven Performer for small gardens and containers.

directions: One of the few truly dwarf rhododendrons with clear lemon-yellow flowers, this mounding shrub opens wavy-lobed blooms in early-to-mid spring above small, neat foliage. It is a regular on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists for its reliable color and compact habit, which suit rock gardens and large containers. Grow it in acidic, sharply drained soil and provide afternoon shade in hotter climates to prevent leaf scorch.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, gritty, well-drained soil; this dwarf lepidote is a long-standing ARS chapter Proven Performer valued for early, abundant bloom.

directions: Masses of funnel-shaped, violet-purple flowers streaked with deeper violet smother this low, cushion-forming shrub in early spring, often before many other rhododendrons begin to color. Its dense habit and cold tolerance have kept it on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists for decades. It suits rock gardens, foundation plantings, and container culture, and prefers acidic, humus-rich soil with excellent drainage.

planting.note: Plant in a sheltered spot in acidic, well-drained soil; this RHS Award of Garden Merit lepidote is an ARS chapter Proven Performer prized for very early bloom in milder climates.

directions: This compact hybrid opens pale pink, darker-shaded flowers as early as late winter, well ahead of most rhododendrons, which makes a sheltered site essential to protect the buds from late frost. It has long appeared on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists in milder regions for its reliable, showy display. Grow it in acidic, well-drained soil out of harsh winter wind, and expect modest size even at maturity.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil; this Shammarello-bred elepidote is a frequently cited ARS chapter Proven Performer valued for fragrance and hardiness.

directions: Bred by Tony Shammarello in Ohio, this vigorous, cold-hardy elepidote produces large, frilly-edged, pale pinkish-mauve flowers brushed with golden-bronze rays and carries a light fragrance unusual among hardy rhododendrons. Its combination of scent and reliable zone 5 hardiness keeps it on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists across the Midwest and Northeast. Plant it in acidic, well-drained soil enriched with organic matter and mulch to protect shallow roots from temperature swings.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this elepidote is a frequently cited ARS chapter Proven Performer known for a bold blotched flower and dependable habit.

directions: Lavender-tinted buds open to crisp white flowers marked with a bold dark red to purple blotch on the upper lobe, giving this sturdy elepidote strong visual contrast in late spring. It has long been recommended on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists for its vigorous, reliable growth and good flower substance. Grow it in acidic, humus-rich, well-drained soil in a site with some afternoon shade.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this semi-dwarf yellow-flowered elepidote is a frequently cited ARS chapter Proven Performer for compact gardens.

directions: Glowing orange buds open to light yellow flowers with a hint of orange shading remaining on the lobes and reverse, creating a warm, two-toned effect on this compact, mounding elepidote. It is regularly named on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists for its manageable size and unusual gold coloring. Grow it in acidic, well-drained soil with partial shade, since it is somewhat less cold-hardy than many large-leaf hybrids.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this historic Slocock-bred elepidote is a long-standing ARS chapter Proven Performer prized for its dense, tidy habit.

directions: Raised by British hybridizer W. C. Slocock before 1934, this old but still widely grown elepidote forms a dense, rounded mound of thick, deep green leaves topped in mid-spring by creamy white flowers flushed pink and flecked with crimson spotting. Its compact habit and attractive foliage have kept it on ARS chapter Proven Performer lists for generations. Plant in acidic, well-drained soil with partial shade and expect slow, steady growth into a tidy specimen shrub.

planting.note: Plant in spring in acidic, well-drained soil; this vigorous, sun-tolerant elepidote is a longtime ARS chapter Proven Performer in the Pacific Northwest.

directions: Tight, conical trusses of reddish-purple flowers with a deep purplish-red blotch cover this thickly foliaged, vigorous elepidote in early summer. Its tolerance for more sun and heat than many hybrids, combined with dependable bloom, has kept it on ARS District 3 and 4 chapter Proven Performer lists for decades. Grow it in acidic, well-drained soil and expect a large, long-lived shrub over time; it tolerates occasional hard pruning to control size.
